query: In conventional alloys, loss of toughness has long been associated with grain-boundary segregation and brittle grain-boundary precipitation. By contrast, compositionally complex high-entropy alloys can suppress rapid grain coarsening and deleterious intermetallic formation and have shown favorable strength–ductility combinations and resistance to high-temperature softening and low-temperature embrittlement. These findings do not establish what governs possible toughness degradation in an initially single-phase high-entropy alloy. Under the constraint of retaining a compositionally complex alloy suitable for demanding engineering service, what testable mechanistic hypothesis explains whether and why brittle behavior emerges? Specify a controlled comparison that would distinguish the hypothesis from conventional-alloy expectations, predicted observations relative to the initial baseline, its service and loading boundaries, supporting prior evidence, and a decisive falsification outcome.

generation.hypothesis: In a single‐phase, compositionally complex high‐entropy alloy, subjecting the material to high strain rate loading under inert (e.g., UHV) conditions induces dynamic grain refinement at high-angle grain boundaries. This process creates an ultra‐nanocrystalline or amorphous-like boundary layer that diminishes intergranular cohesion through cavitation/decohesion, resulting in brittle fracture that is distinct from conventional impurity segregation or intermetallic precipitation mechanisms.
generation.material_initial_state: An as-processed, coarse-grained, single-phase high-entropy alloy known for high toughness and ductility.
generation.intervention: Subjecting the alloy to controlled high-strain rate mechanical loading (such as high-rate sliding or tensile tests) under inert or ultra-high vacuum conditions.
generation.conditions: Room or moderately low temperatures where thermal diffusion is minimal, ensuring that the loading is the dominant driver the dynamic microstructure change in an inert environment.
generation.structural_mediator: The formation of an ultra-nanocrystalline or dynamically amorphized layer localized at high-angle grain boundaries.
generation.mechanism: High strain rate loading reduces the effective grain size below a critical threshold, suppressing conventional dislocation-mediated plasticity and promoting grain-boundary sliding. This shift triggers cavitation and decohesion at the refined boundaries, thereby reducing ductility and leading to brittle failure.
generation.predicted_outcome: Relative to the coarse-grained baseline, the alloy subjected to high strain rate loading will exhibit significantly reduced ductility and increased intergranular cracking along with microstructural evidence (via TEM/STEM) of an ultra-fine or amorphous boundary layer. This brittle behavior will occur without the presence of chemical segregation or intermetallic precipitates.
generation.baseline: The as-prepared coarse-grained alloy, which under conventional low strain rate loading demonstrates high toughness and ductility.
generation.boundary: This hypothesis is expected to hold under conditions of high strain rate loading at room or moderately low temperatures in an inert atmosphere; it may not apply at elevated temperatures where diffusion-driven chemical segregation or precipitate formation becomes significant.
generation.uncertainty: The precise critical grain size triggering the transition and the quantitative contribution of cavitation to the loss of ductility remain to be determined.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare identical samples of the single-phase HEA with a known coarse-grained microstructure. Subject one set to high-strain rate mechanical loading under ultra-high vacuum conditions to induce dynamic grain refinement, while keeping a control set under low-strain rate loading in the same inert atmosphere. Following deformation, perform high-resolution microstructural characterization (e.g., TEM, STEM) to assess the grain boundary features and use mechanical tests (tensile, fracture toughness) to evaluate ductility and cracking modes.
measurements: Grain size distribution and evidence of dynamic amorphization at grain boundaries (via TEM/STEM)
Fractography to identify intergranular versus transgranular fracture modes
Mechanical properties measurements such as ductility (elongation to failure) and fracture toughness
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the high-strain rate loaded samples do not exhibit a statistically significant reduction in near-boundary grain size or formation of an amorphous layer, and if their ductility and fracture behavior remain comparable to the low-strain rate control (i.e., no increase in intergranular cracking or brittle features), then the hypothesis that dynamic grain refinement and associated cavitation at grain boundaries induce brittleness is falsified.

cited_evidence.text: AbstractWe present evidence of inverse Hall-Petch behavior for a single-phase high entropy alloy (CoCrFeMnNi) in ultra-high vacuum and show that it is associated with low friction coefficients (~0.3). Grain size measurements by STEM validate a recently proposed dynamic amorphization model that accurately predicts grain size-dependent shear strength in the inverse Hall-Petch regime. Wear rates in the initially soft (coarse grained) material were shown to be remarkably low (~10–6 mm3/N-m), the lowest for any HEA tested in an inert environment where oxidation and the formation of mixed metal-oxide films is mitigated. The combined high wear resistance and low friction are linked to the formation of an ultra-nanocrystalline near-surface layer. The dynamic amorphization model was also used to predict an average high angle grain boundary energy (0.87 J/m2). This value was used to explain cavitation-induced nanoporosity found in the highly deformed surface layer, a phenomenon that has been linked to superplasticity.Subject terms: Structural materials, Structural properties

drafts.hypothesis: In a single‐phase high‐entropy alloy, prolonged exposure to moderate, service-like thermal conditions and cyclic mechanical loading causes local atomic ordering and clustering—particularly near grain boundaries—that weakens the grain boundary cohesion and induces a brittle response. This mechanism is distinct from the typical large-scale grain-boundary segregation and intermetallic precipitation observed in conventional alloys.
drafts.material_initial_state: An as-homogenized, single-phase, disordered high-entropy alloy (e.g., an equiatomic multi-principal element alloy with a uniform grain structure)
drafts.intervention: Subject the alloy to controlled thermal aging at intermediate temperatures combined with cyclic mechanical loading to simulate service conditions
drafts.conditions: Temperatures sufficiently high to activate limited atomic diffusion (but not high enough to drive large-scale intermetallic phase formation) and cyclic stresses that mimic realistic in-service loading cycles
drafts.structural_mediator: Emergence of localized atomic ordering and elemental clustering at grain boundaries and within grains
drafts.mechanism: Under thermal and mechanical stimuli, subtle elemental partitioning and reordering occur within the otherwise disordered matrix. The resulting nanoscale ordered clusters, particularly along grain boundaries, serve as stress concentrators and reduce the cohesive strength across those boundaries, leading to premature crack initiation and a reduction in toughness.
drafts.predicted_outcome: Compared to the baseline fully disordered state, the treated alloy will exhibit measurable reductions in toughness and ductility (e.g., lower fracture toughness and higher brittleness in impact tests) without the emergence of coarse intermetallic precipitates typical of conventional alloys.
drafts.baseline: The initial state of the high-entropy alloy in a fully disordered, single-phase condition without induced local ordering
drafts.boundary: This mechanism is expected to be operative under moderate high-temperature and cyclic loading conditions typical of demanding engineering service. It may not occur in regimes where either the thermal activation is too low to promote atomic diffusion or excessively high temperatures lead to other dominant degradation mechanisms such as significant grain growth or coarse-scale precipitate formation.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare identical samples of the target high-entropy alloy. Divide them into two groups: a control group maintained at baseline conditions and an experimental group exposed to the specified thermal aging and cyclic mechanical loading. In parallel, conduct the same treatment on a conventional alloy known to degrade via coarse grain-boundary segregation and intermetallic precipitation. Analyze the microstructure (using TEM and atom probe tomography) for signs of local ordering/clustering and perform fracture toughness and impact tests on all samples.
measurements: Microstructural characterization (TEM, atom probe tomography) to detect nanoclusters and local ordering
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the experimentally treated high-entropy alloy does not show detectable local ordering/clustering at grain boundaries—i.e., if no significant difference in microstructure and toughness is observed relative to the baseline—or if the degradation mirrors the formation of coarse intermetallics as seen in conventional alloys, then the hypothesis would be falsified.

drafts.hypothesis: In an initially single‐phase, compositionally complex high-entropy alloy, service or loading conditions (thermal and/or mechanical) can induce localized short‐range ordering that triggers nanoscale, intragranular precipitation of a brittle intermetallic phase. This localized phase formation depletes the ductile matrix near high-stress regions and leads to brittle behavior, distinguishing its mechanism from conventional grain boundary segregation and precipitation.
drafts.material_initial_state: A single-phase, compositionally complex high-entropy alloy with a random solid solution microstructure.
drafts.intervention: Subject the alloy to controlled high-temperature and/or high-strain cyclic loading conditions that simulate service environments.
drafts.conditions: Service-like conditions where the temperature and strain levels are sufficient to activate diffusion and the rearrangement of atoms (e.g., elevated temperatures combined with mechanical loading), but below the melting/phase transformation thresholds.
drafts.structural_mediator: Nanoscale, intragranular precipitates (or clusters) that emerge due to locally enhanced short-range order under stress.
drafts.mechanism: Enhanced local diffusion and stress-assisted short-range ordering during service promote the nucleation of brittle intermetallic precipitates within grains (rather than along grain boundaries). This localized phase separation diminishes toughness in the high-stress regions by locally reducing ductility and resistance to crack propagation.
drafts.predicted_outcome: Tough samples will initially exhibit a homogeneous microstructure, while exposed samples that develop brittle behavior will show localized nanoscale precipitate formation, particularly in high-strain zones. Mechanical testing will reveal reduced toughness and a shift from ductile to brittle fracture modes in these areas compared to the baseline.
drafts.baseline: The as-processed, homogeneous single-phase state of the high-entropy alloy without evidence of nanoscale ordering or precipitation.
drafts.boundary: The hypothesis applies under service conditions involving elevated temperatures combined with mechanical loading. It may not hold outside these boundaries (e.g., very low temperatures where diffusion is suppressed or extremely high stresses that trigger other failure mechanisms).

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare samples of the high-entropy alloy in the as-processed (baseline) state. Subject a set of samples to service-like loading conditions (controlled high-temperature and cyclic or sustained mechanical loading) while keeping a control set under inert thermal conditions with no mechanical stress. Use high-resolution transmission electron microscopy (TEM) and atom probe tomography (APT) to characterize the microstructure, focusing on nanoscale precipitate (or cluster) formation. Additionally, perform mechanical toughness tests and fracture surface analyses to correlate observed microstructural changes with fracture modes.
measurements: TEM imaging to detect nanoscale precipitates or ordering
Atom probe tomography for local compositional analysis
Mechanical toughness and ductility tests (e.g., fracture toughness testing)
Fractography to assess brittle versus ductile failure modes
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: The hypothesis will be falsified if (a) under service-like conditions no detectable nanoscale, intragranular precipitates or ordering is found in regions associated with brittle fracture, or (b) brittle behavior correlates exclusively with traditional grain boundary segregation or precipitation, with no intragranular changes relative to the baseline.

drafts.hypothesis: In a single‐phase high-entropy alloy, when subjected to high strain rates under conditions that limit thermally activated segregation (e.g. in ultra‐high vacuum and at room or moderately low temperatures), the deformation induces extreme grain refinement at the surface. This leads to the formation of an ultra‐nanocrystalline or dynamically amorphized layer along high-angle grain boundaries, which in turn weakens intergranular cohesion (via cavitation/decohesion) and triggers brittle failure. This mechanism is distinct from conventional alloys where brittleness is typically due to impurity segregation or intermetallic precipitates.
drafts.material_initial_state: An initially coarse-grained, single-phase high-entropy alloy (e.g., equiatomic CoCrFeMnNi) with minimal grain-boundary segregation.
drafts.intervention: Subjecting the material to controlled high-strain rate sliding or deformation testing under ultra-high vacuum conditions.
drafts.conditions: Room or moderately low temperatures, high strain-rate loading, and an inert (oxide-free) environment to eliminate chemical effects like segregation or precipitation.
drafts.structural_mediator: A dynamically generated ultra-nanocrystalline/amorphous layer localized at grain boundaries produced by extreme grain refinement.
drafts.mechanism: The high strain rate leads to a transition from dislocation plasticity to grain-boundary sliding as the grain size decreases below a critical value. This transition suppresses conventional intragranular deformation and promotes grain-boundary cavitation/decohesion, resulting in premature brittle failure despite the absence of impurity-induced embrittlement.
drafts.predicted_outcome: Compared to the baseline (initial coarse-grained alloy with good ductility), the alloy after high-strain rate deformation will exhibit significantly reduced ductility and increased intergranular cracking, with evidence of a refined (nano-scale/amorphized) surface layer. This brittle behavior is not attributed to grain-boundary segregation or intermetallic precipitation.
drafts.baseline: The as-prepared single-phase HEA in a coarse-grained state shows high toughness and ductility under conventional deformation conditions.
drafts.boundary: This hypothesized mechanism is expected to dominate under high-strain rate, low-temperature (or modestly heated) conditions with minimal thermal activation (and hence minimal chemical segregation); it may not apply if the service temperature is high enough for diffusion-driven segregation or precipitation to occur.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare two sets of single-phase HEA samples with similar initial microstructures. One set undergoes high-strain rate sliding testing in ultra-high vacuum, while the control set experiences low-strain rate deformation under otherwise identical inert conditions. Post-test, characterize the near-surface grain size and structure via STEM/TEM, and compare tensile ductility and fracture modes.
measurements: Grain size distribution and evidence of amorphization (using STEM/TEM)
Fractography to detect intergranular versus transgranular fracture features
Quantitative measurements of ductility (e.g., elongation to failure) and strength
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the high-strain rate samples do not show a statistically significant reduction in grain size (or evidence of dynamic amorphization) at grain boundaries, and if their ductility and fracture behavior remain comparable to the low-strain rate control (i.e., no increase in intergranular cracking is observed), then the hypothesis that dynamic grain refinement triggers brittle behavior is falsified.

drafts.hypothesis: In an initially single‐phase high-entropy alloy, brittle behavior can emerge not because of impurity segregation or intermetallic precipitation but because high-strain rate or localized shear conditions induce a dynamic refinement of the grain structure—particularly at high-angle grain boundaries—leading to ultrafine (nano‐scale) grain boundary formation that reduces interfacial cohesion and promotes cavitation-induced decohesion.
drafts.material_initial_state: A compositionally complex, single-phase high-entropy alloy (e.g., equiatomic CoCrFeMnNi) with a relatively coarse grain structure and no significant grain-boundary segregation or intermetallic precipitates.
drafts.intervention: Subject the alloy to controlled mechanical loading (e.g., high strain rate tensile or sliding contact) under an inert or ultra-high vacuum environment that minimizes temperature increases and impurity effects, thereby inducing dynamic grain refinement in the near-surface or localized deformation regions.
drafts.conditions: Service conditions that combine high shear or strain rate at moderate temperatures (where thermal effects do not induce impurity segregation) in an inert atmosphere (e.g. UHV) so that only mechanically driven grain refinement occurs.
drafts.structural_mediator: The formation of an ultra-nanocrystalline layer at high-angle grain boundaries accompanied by cavitation/nanoporosity that reduces the cohesive strength of the boundaries.
drafts.mechanism: Under high strain rates, dislocation activity is suppressed when grain sizes are refined below a critical value (inverse Hall-Petch regime), promoting grain boundary sliding and dynamic amorphization. This leads to a reduction in grain boundary cohesion through cavitation, with localized stress concentrations initiating brittle intergranular cracking even in the absence of impurity segregation.
drafts.predicted_outcome: Compared to the initial coarse-grained baseline, samples that develop an ultrafine near-boundary grain structure under high shear will exhibit reduced ductility and a brittle fracture mode characterized by grain-boundary cavitation and decohesion, despite retaining a single-phase solid solution.
drafts.baseline: The HEA in its as-processed, coarse-grained, single-phase state displays favorable toughness with ductile behavior under conventional loading conditions.
drafts.boundary: This brittle transition is expected only within a window of high strain rate (or localized high shear) and moderate temperature in inert environments; under low strain rate or at temperatures that favor grain growth, the alloy should retain its baseline toughness.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare two sets of samples from an identical single-phase HEA. In one set, induce dynamic shear loading (e.g., via high strain rate tensile or sliding tests in UHV) known to cause severe grain refinement. In the other set, pre-anneal the material to stabilize a moderately coarse grain structure before applying the same mechanical load. Use in-situ TEM or high-resolution STEM to monitor grain-boundary structure evolution and cavitation. Concurrently perform macroscopic mechanical tests to assess ductility and fracture modes.
measurements: Grain size distribution and evolution at or near grain boundaries during deformation
Occurrence and extent of nanoporosity/cavitation at grain boundaries
Fracture surface analysis to determine intergranular versus transgranular fracture modes
Stress-strain response (ductility, yield strength, and fracture toughness)
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If both sample sets (dynamically refined and pre-stabilized coarse-grain) exhibit similar ductility and fracture modes with no enhanced signs of grain-boundary cavitation or intergranular cracking under identical inert and loading conditions, then the hypothesis that dynamic strain-induced ultrafine grain-boundary formation is responsible for brittle behavior is falsified.
